summary: Sets the architectural assumptions for mapping between SIP and XMPP, two protocols used for messaging and presence. It also specifies how addresses and error conditions are mapped between the two. It is the foundation for other mapping documents.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP and XMPP are two different ways of doing presence and messaging. This RFC describes the gateway that sits between them, how a name in one system is rewritten as a name in the other, and how a failure on one side is reported on the other.

subtitle: The ground rules for letting a SIP user talk to an XMPP user across a gateway.

tldr.problem: SIP and XMPP both carry presence, messaging and session setup, and both are widely deployed. Neither protocol can talk to the other, so the two worlds are separate.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC sets the architectural assumptions, gives the algorithms for turning an address in one protocol into an address in the other, and provides tables for mapping XMPP error conditions to SIP response codes and back.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the first document in a series; the others cover presence, messaging and media sessions.

today: RFC 7247 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the first document in the series: the others cover presence, messaging and media sessions, and this one sets the architecture, the address mapping and the error mapping that they build on.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IETF has worked on two signalling technologies that can be used for multimedia session negotiation, instant messaging, presence, capabilities discovery, notifications and other functions served by real-time communication applications. The first is the Session Initiation Protocol of RFC 3261, along with the extensions developed in the SIMPLE working group. The second is the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol of RFC 6120, along with the various XMPP extensions developed by the IETF and by the XMPP Standards Foundation.

Because these technologies are widely deployed, it is important to clearly define mappings between them for the sake of interworking. This document provides the basis for a series of SIP-XMPP interworking specifications by defining architectural assumptions, address translation methods and error condition mappings. Other documents in the series define mappings for presence, messaging and media sessions.

The guidelines in this series are based on implementation and deployment experience, and they describe techniques that have worked well in the field with existing systems. In practice, interworking has been achieved through direct protocol mappings, not through mapping to an abstract model as described in RFC 3859 and RFC 3860. This series therefore describes the direct mapping approach in enough detail for developers of new implementations to achieve practical interworking between SIP systems and XMPP systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC deliberately maps one protocol onto the other directly, rather than inventing a middle model that both would have to be translated into. That is how real deployments work, so that is what is written down here.

sections.title: Architectural Assumptions
sections.content:
Protocol translation between SIP and XMPP could occur in a number of different entities, depending on the architecture of real-time communication deployments. It could occur within a multiprotocol server, which uses protocol-specific connection managers to initiate traffic to and accept traffic from clients or other servers natively using SIP, XMPP and so on. It could occur within a multiprotocol client, which enables a user to establish connections natively with various servers. Or it could occur within a gateway that acts as a dedicated protocol translator, taking one protocol as input and providing another protocol as output.

This document assumes that the protocol translation will occur within a gateway. When information needs to flow from an XMPP-based system to a SIP-based system, translation occurs within an XMPP-to-SIP gateway that translates XMPP syntax and semantics on behalf of an XMPP server, and these two logical functions together comprise an XMPP service. When information needs to flow from a SIP-based system to an XMPP-based system, translation occurs within a SIP-to-XMPP gateway that translates SIP syntax and semantics on behalf of a SIP server, and together these comprise a SIP service. Naturally these logical functions could occur in one and the same actual entity; the RFC differentiates between them mainly for explanatory purposes.

The assumption is not meant to discourage protocol translation within multiprotocol clients or servers. It is followed mainly to clarify the discussion and examples, so that the principles can be more easily understood and applied by client and server implementors with appropriate modifications to the examples and terminology.

The document assumes that a gateway will translate directly from one protocol to the other. For the sake of the examples it further assumes that translation occurs within a gateway in the source domain, so that information generated by the user of an XMPP system is translated by a gateway within the trust domain of that XMPP system, and information generated by the user of a SIP system is translated by a gateway within the trust domain of that SIP system. Nothing in the document ought to be taken as recommending against translation at the destination domain.

The example deployment in the RFC's Figure 1 has romeo@example.net as a SIP user, example.net as a SIP server with an associated SIP-to-XMPP gateway, juliet@example.com as an XMPP user, and example.com as an XMPP server with an associated XMPP-to-SIP gateway. Note that bidirectional communication between the SIP server and the XMPP server can be established over either SIP or XMPP. If the XMPP user initiates the interaction, the XMPP server invokes its XMPP-to-SIP gateway, so the communication occurs over SIP. If the SIP user initiates the interaction, the SIP server invokes its SIP-to-XMPP gateway, so the communication occurs over XMPP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side has its own gateway sitting next to its server. Whichever side starts the conversation, that side's gateway does the translating, and the message then travels on in the other protocol.

sections.title: Interdomain Federation
sections.content:
The architectural assumptions imply that communication between a SIP system and an XMPP system takes place using interdomain federation. The SIP server invokes its associated SIP-to-XMPP gateway, which communicates with the XMPP server using native XMPP server-to-server methods. Similarly, the XMPP server invokes its associated XMPP-to-SIP gateway, which communicates with the SIP server using native SIP server-to-server methods.

When an XMPP server receives an XMPP stanza whose to address specifies or includes a domain other than its own, it needs to determine whether the destination domain communicates via XMPP or SIP. To do so it performs one or more DNS SRV lookups of RFC 2782 for _xmpp-server records, as specified in RFC 6120. If the response returns a hostname the XMPP server can attempt XMPP communication. If not, it can determine the appropriate location for SIP communication at the target domain using the procedures of RFC 3263.

Similarly, when a SIP server receives a SIP message whose Request-URI or To header specifies or includes a domain other than its own, it uses the procedures of RFC 3263. If that response returns a hostname the SIP server can attempt SIP communication. If not, it can perform one or more DNS SRV lookups for _xmpp-server records as specified in RFC 6120.

In both cases the server might have previously determined that the foreign domain communicates via SIP or XMPP, in which case it would not need to perform the relevant DNS lookups. Caching of such information is a matter of implementation and local service policy and is therefore out of scope.

Existing SIP and XMPP server implementations do not typically include the ability to communicate using the other technology. One common architectural pattern is to associate a gateway with the core server implementation, in XMPP such a gateway might be called a connection manager. How exactly such a gateway interacts with the core server to complete tasks such as address lookups and communication with systems that use the other technology is a matter of implementation.

Because RFC 6120 specifies a binding of XMPP to TCP, a gateway from SIP to XMPP will need to support TCP as the underlying transport protocol. By contrast, either TCP or UDP can be used as the underlying transport for SIP messages, and a given SIP deployment might support only UDP, so a gateway from XMPP to SIP might need to communicate with a SIP server using either TCP or UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that gets a message for another domain has to work out which protocol that other domain speaks. It looks up the _xmpp-server DNS record: if a hostname comes back the other side speaks XMPP, and if not the server falls back to the usual SIP lookup.

sections.title: Address Formats and What Is In Scope
sections.content:
The basic SIP address format is a sip or sips URI. When a SIP entity supports extensions for instant messaging it might be identified by an im URI, as specified in the Common Profile for Instant Messaging, and when it supports extensions for presence it might be identified by a pres URI, as specified in the Common Profile for Presence. SIP entities typically also support the tel URI scheme and might support other URI schemes as well.

The XMPP address format is specified in RFC 6122, although XMPP URIs are not used natively on the XMPP network. RFC 6121 encourages instant messaging and presence applications of XMPP to also support im and pres URIs, although such support might simply involve leaving resolution of such addresses up to an XMPP server.

The RFC primarily describes mappings for addresses of the form user@domain, and also provides guidelines for mapping the addresses of specific user agent instances, which take the form of Globally Routable User Agent URIs in SIP and resourceparts in XMPP. Mapping of protocol-specific identifiers, such as telephone numbers, is out of scope. Mapping of domain names is also out of scope for now, since that is a matter for the Domain Name System: the issue for interworking between SIP and XMPP relates to the translation of fully internationalized domain names, which are not allowed in the SIP address format but are allowed in the XMPP address. The RFC therefore focuses primarily on the local part of an address, secondarily on the instance-specific part, and not at all on the domain-name part.

The sip and sips, im and pres, and XMPP address schemes allow different sets of characters, although all three allow alphanumeric characters and disallow both spaces and control characters. In some cases characters allowed in one scheme are disallowed in others, and these characters need to be mapped appropriately to ensure interworking across systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The two protocols allow different characters in the name part of an address, and even disagree on whether a slash or an ampersand may appear. The domain part is left alone, because that is the DNS's business, and only the name and the device part are translated here.

sections.title: Local Part Mapping
sections.content:
The local part of a sip or sips URI inherits from the userinfo rule of RFC 3986 with several changes. The RFC discusses the SIP user rule, which is one or more unreserved, escaped or user-unreserved characters, where user-unreserved covers the ampersand, equals, plus, dollar, comma, semicolon, question mark and slash, and unreserved covers alphanumerics and marks, which are the hyphen, underscore, period, exclamation mark, tilde, asterisk, apostrophe and the parentheses.

For the im and pres URIs the RFC makes the simplifying assumption that the local part inherits from the dot-atom-text rule of RFC 5322 rather than the more complicated local-part rule, so it allows alphanumerics and a set of punctuation characters.

The local part of an XMPP address allows any ASCII character except space, control characters, and the ampersand, apostrophe, slash, colon, less-than, greater-than and at-sign characters.

The table below lists the allowed and disallowed characters in the local part of identifiers for each protocol, aside from the alphanumeric, space and control characters. When transforming the local part of an address from one address format to another, an application should proceed as follows. First, unescape any escaped characters in the source address, for example unescaping %23 to a hash from SIP to XMPP, and unescaping a backslash-27 to an apostrophe from XMPP to SIP. Second, leave unmodified any characters that are allowed in the destination scheme. Third, escape any characters that are allowed in the source scheme but reserved in the destination scheme, as escaping is defined for the destination scheme. Where the destination scheme is a URI, each reserved character must be percent-encoded to the form %hexhex as specified in Section 2.5 of RFC 3986. Where the destination scheme is a native XMPP address, each reserved character must be encoded to a backslash followed by hexhex as specified in XEP-0106.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is: undo the escaping the source protocol used, keep the characters the destination protocol allows, and re-escape the rest in the way the destination protocol expects. A URI uses percent signs, an XMPP address uses a backslash.

sections.title: Mapping in Both Directions
sections.content:
The meaning of a resourcepart in XMPP, the portion of a Jabber ID after the slash character, matches that of a Globally Routable User Agent URI in SIP. In both cases these constructs identify a particular device associated with the bare JID of an XMPP entity or with the Address of Record of a SIP entity, so it is reasonable to map the value of a gr URI parameter to an XMPP resourcepart and the other way round. The mapping does not apply to temporary GRUUs, only to GRUUs associated with an Address of Record.

SIP to XMPP. The high-level algorithm is to remove the URI scheme, split at the first at-sign into local part and hostname, translate any percent-encoded strings to percent-decoded octets, treat the result as a UTF-8 string, translate the ampersand, apostrophe and slash to their escaped forms, optionally apply the Nodeprep profile of stringprep or its replacement for canonicalization, recombine the local part with the mapped hostname to form a bare JID, and, if the SIP address contained a gr URI parameter, append a slash and the gr value to form a full JID.

XMPP to SIP. The high-level algorithm is to split the XMPP address into localpart, domainpart and resourcepart, optionally apply the Nodeprep profile of stringprep or its replacement for canonicalization of the localpart, translate the escaped forms back to the ampersand, apostrophe and slash, determine whether the foreign domain supports im and pres URIs, discovered by a DNS SRV lookup as specified in RFC 6121, and otherwise assume that it supports sip and sips URIs. Then, if converting into an im or pres URI, percent-encode each byte in the set of parentheses, comma, semicolon, period and square brackets, and any UTF-8 character outside the ASCII range. If converting into a sip or sips URI, percent-encode each byte in the set of hash, percent, square brackets, caret, backtick, brace and pipe, and any UTF-8 character outside the ASCII range. Combine the resulting local part with the mapped hostname, prepend the scheme, and, if the XMPP address included a resourcepart and the destination scheme is sip or sips, optionally append the resourcepart as the gr URI parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP to XMPP, the address is decoded, three characters are re-escaped for XMPP, and a device identifier moves from the gr parameter into the part after the slash. Going the other way, the same steps run in reverse and a device identifier moves back into the gr parameter.

sections.title: Error Mapping
sections.content:
Various differences between XMPP error conditions and SIP response codes make it hard to provide a comprehensive and consistent mapping. The set of XMPP error conditions is fixed in the core XMPP specification and supplemented where needed by application-specific extensions, while the set of SIP response codes is more open to change. XMPP has defined fewer error conditions related to stanza handling, 22 of them in RFC 6120, than SIP has defined response codes related to message handling, 71 SIP response codes being registered with IANA at the date of writing. In many cases the SIP response codes are more specific than the XMPP error conditions: from an XMPP perspective the SIP codes 413 Request Entity Too Large and 414 Request-URI Too Long are simply two different types of response to the same bad request. And SIP differentiates between responses about a particular endpoint or resource in the 4xx series and responses about a user, all of a user's endpoints or resources, in the 6xx series. There is no such distinction in XMPP, since the same error condition can be returned in relation to the bare JID of a user or the full JID of a particular endpoint, depending on the to address of the original request.

As a result of these and other factors, the mapping of error conditions and response codes is more of an art than a science. The RFC provides suggested mappings, but implementations are free to deviate if needed. Also, because no XMPP error conditions are equivalent to the provisional 1xx and successful 2xx response codes in SIP, the RFC suggests mappings only for the redirection 3xx, request failure 4xx, server failure 5xx and global failure 6xx families.

Supplementary information about SIP response codes can be expressed in the Reason-Phrase in the Status-Line header, and detailed information about XMPP error conditions can be expressed in the text child of the error element. Although the semantics of these constructs are specified in a slightly different way, it is reasonable for a gateway to map them to each other if they are found in a SIP response or XMPP error stanza.

The tables below give the suggested mappings. Notes attached to the tables explain the cases where two codes are offered. Where the error relates to a full JID with a resourcepart, the 4xx code is recommended, and where it relates to a bare JID, the 6xx code. Where the gone element includes character data naming a new address it must be mapped to 301, and otherwise to 410. The remote-server-not-found error can mean that the remote server either does not exist or cannot be resolved, and SIP has 404 and 408 for those two cases. The service-unavailable error is widely used to say that the intended recipient does not support the feature, that a server cannot perform the requested service, or to avoid disclosing whether an account exists, which is quite different from the SIP 503 response, so mapping it to 503 is not recommended; 403 and 405 are closest in meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: The two protocols do not have the same errors, so this is a set of suggestions rather than a strict rule. The tricky part is that SIP distinguishes a problem with one device from a problem with the whole user, and XMPP does not, so the same XMPP error can map to a 4xx or a 6xx code depending on which address was used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Detailed security considerations for SIP and XMPP are given in RFC 3261 and RFC 6120 respectively. To protect information sent between SIP and XMPP systems, deployed gateways should use Transport Layer Security when communicating over TCP and Datagram Transport Layer Security when communicating over UDP.

A To header or a Request-URI containing a Session Initiation Protocol Secure URI is used to indicate that all hops in a communication path need to be protected using TLS. Because XMPP lacks a way to signal that all hops need to be protected, if the To header or Request-URI of a SIP message is a SIPS URI then the SIP-to-XMPP gateway must not translate the SIP message into an XMPP stanza and must not route it to the destination XMPP server. There might be exceptions to such a policy, such as explicit agreement among two operators to enforce per-hop security, but currently they are quite rare.

A gateway between SIP and XMPP in either direction effectively acts as a SIP back-to-back user agent. The amplification vulnerability described in RFC 5393 can manifest itself with such gateways, and a gateway should implement the loop-detection methods defined in that specification to help mitigate the possibility of amplification attacks. Although it would be possible to signal the Max-Forwards and Max-Breadth SIP headers over XMPP using the Stanza Headers and Internet Metadata extension, that extension is not widely implemented, so defenses against excessive looping and amplification attacks when messages pass back and forth through SIP and XMPP networks are out of scope for this document. Implementations are strongly encouraged to incorporate appropriate countermeasures wherever possible.

The ability to use a wide range of Unicode characters can lead to security issues, especially the possibility of user confusion over identifiers containing visually similar characters, also called confusables. The PRECIS framework describes some of these security issues, and additional guidance can be found in the Unicode Security Mechanisms document.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things to watch. A SIP request marked as needing encryption on every hop cannot be carried into XMPP at all, because XMPP has no way to say that. And a gateway can be used to amplify traffic between the two networks, so it should detect loops the way the SIP documents describe.
